hook_text: In 1957, a metal ball the size of a beach ball made the most powerful country on Earth panic. Why?
clip_script: October 1957. Radios around the world pick up a strange beep. It is Sputnik, the first satellite, launched by the Soviet Union. Americans are stunned. If a Soviet rocket can reach space, it can reach American cities. The space race is on. The Soviets keep winning: the first dog in orbit, the first man in space, Yuri Gagarin, the first woman, the first spacewalk. So in 1961 President Kennedy sets an almost impossible goal: put a man on the Moon before 1970. Four hundred thousand people go to work. There are tragedies along the way. Then, on 20 July 1969, Neil Armstrong steps onto the Moon. Six hundred million people watch. In 1975 the rivals shake hands in orbit. And down here, a dish near Johannesburg helped listen to the spacecraft. The race began with fear. It ended with footprints.
visual_style: A small silver sphere with antennas crossing a starry sky; a newspaper headline; a cosmonaut smiling in a helmet; a giant rocket lifting off; a boot print in grey dust; two spacecraft docking; a large radio dish in the Gauteng hills.
pacing: Quick sequence of firsts, a pause for the landing, gentle close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to understand the space race and why it mattered in the Cold War.
